name: Konbaung Dynasty (Burma)
summary: The last dynasty to rule Burma. It created the second-largest empire in Burmese history but lost three wars to Britain, ending the Burmese monarchy in 1885.

location.value: Burma (the infobox gives 794,000 km² in 1824), with Arakan taken in 1784, Manipur in 1814 and Assam in 1817.

terrain.value: The Irrawaddy valley, hills and the coast.

climate.value: Monsoon, with heavy rain on the coast and a dry central zone around Mandalay.

resources.value: Rice, teak, rubies, jade (traded to China) and oil.

population.value: About 3,000,000 in 1824 (infobox), below the entry’s estimate of about 4 million.

urbanisation.value: Royal capitals moved several times; Mandalay was founded in 1857.

migration.value: War captives from Siam and Manipur were resettled.

economicBase.value: Commercial reforms stabilised government income: the kyat was introduced in 1852 and a system of cash taxes and salaries with standard silver coinage began in 1857. Teak and gems are not covered in the part read.

tradeRoutes.value: Overland trade with Yunnan (China) and sea trade with British India.

wealth.value: No estimate is possible for this period.

moneyAndTax.value: Silver by weight until King Mindon introduced coins (1865).

inequality.value: Royal court above commoners and hereditary service groups.

governmentType.value: An absolute monarchy based on Buddhist kingship.

keyRulers.value: Alaungpaya founded the dynasty in 1752; Hsinbyushin (1763–1776) took Ayutthaya in 1767; Bodawpaya (1782–1819); Mindon (1853–1878); Thibaw (1878–1885), the last king.

succession.value: Hereditary, but often violent, with killings of rival princes.

institutions.value: Continued the administrative reforms begun by the Toungoo dynasty, laying the foundations of the modern state of Burma.

stability.value: Strong early; weakened by wars with Britain.

eliteConflict.value: Palace massacres of princes at successions, such as in 1879.

armyAndTech.value: Large armies; firearms; later outgunned by Britain.

majorWars.value: Destroyed Ayutthaya (1767); lost three Anglo-Burmese Wars (1824–1885).

territoryChange.value: The second-largest empire in Burmese history.

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals included Siam, Qing China and Britain.

inventions.value: Little is known; King Mindon built modern factories and a telegraph.

scienceEducation.value: Monastic schools gave high literacy among men.

openness.value: Mindon sent students abroad and built factories.

communicationTransport.value: Boats on the Irrawaddy; King Mindon introduced a telegraph and steamships.

religion.value: Theravada Buddhism was the official religion; Mindon hosted the Fifth Buddhist synod in 1872 (the entry said 1871).

artsArchitecture.value: Mandalay Palace and the Kuthodaw Pagoda (“world’s largest book”).

socialStructure.value: King, nobles, monks, commoners and slaves.

dailyLife.value: Wooden houses on stilts; rice, ngapi (fish paste) and tea-leaf salad.

neighbours.value: Siam, Qing China, Manipur, Assam and British India.

ideasReligions.value: Theravada Buddhism; the Kuthodaw Pagoda holds the whole Buddhist canon carved on stone.

colonisation.value: Defeated by Britain; Burma became part of British India.

peakPeriod.value: The page calls the dynasty’s peak extent the second-largest empire in Burmese history (794,000 km² in 1824); Ayutthaya fell in 1767.

declineSignals.value: Defeats in the Anglo-Burmese Wars (1824–26, 1852) cost it its coasts.

outcome.value: Britain ended the monarchy in 1885 and exiled King Thibaw.

sources.value: Burmese chronicles and British records. Checked against Wikipedia (“Konbaung dynasty”).

knownFor.label: Kuthodaw Pagoda
knownFor.note: Buddhist scriptures carved on 729 stone slabs.
